# Plan: Rebuild the Goodreads Book Recommender

## Context
The 2023 app (a copy lives in `New & Improved Goodreads Book Recommender/`) takes about a minute per request. It reloads roughly 650 MB of data and refits KNN over 245k users every time. It only accepts a Goodreads CSV, and its genre labels are LDA word lists. The goal is a fast, modern web app that uses the **same UCSD Goodreads data** and offers two input flows:
1. upload a Goodreads export CSV;
2. search titles and rate them 1–5 stars for quick recommendations.

It keeps inferred genres (with descriptive names), the similar-readers lists, and book covers.

**Decisions made:**
- Method: hybrid of precomputed similar books (item-item) and book vectors with fold-in (ALS).
- Stack: FastAPI with a React + Vite + TS frontend.
- Data: ratings from `reviews_dedup`, with the ratings stage swappable for `interactions_dedup` later.
- Genres: mined from `popular_shelves`, with the shelf→genre YAML drafted by an LLM and reviewed by the user.
- Old notebooks and `Web App/` get **deleted** from the copy. The original folder keeps them.

**Environment limits:** M3 laptop with 8 GB RAM and Python 3.9. So: use uv with Python 3.12, stream the gz JSON (never decompress to disk), and compute item similarity in chunks.

## Layout (inside `New & Improved Goodreads Book Recommender/`)
```
pyproject.toml   Makefile   Dockerfile   CLAUDE.md (rewrite)
config/pipeline.yaml          # thresholds + hyperparams
config/shelf_genres.yaml      # shelf -> display name + parent genre (LLM-drafted, reviewed)
src/goodrec/core/             # textnorm, scoring, similar_readers, artifacts (shared by api + eval)
src/goodrec/pipeline/         # s00..s10 scripts + streaming io
src/goodrec/eval/             # splits, metrics, run
src/goodrec/api/              # FastAPI main, routes, schemas, matching, search
frontend/                     # Vite + React + TS -> dist served by FastAPI
tests/ (+ tests/fixtures/goodreads_library_export.csv, taken from the old data before deletion)
data/raw, data/interim, artifacts/   # gitignored; artifacts published to GCS/GitHub Release
```
Delete: `00_*.ipynb`, `01_*.ipynb`, `02_*.ipynb`, `Web App/`, `__pycache__/`. Keep the sample export CSV as a test fixture.

## Offline pipeline (idempotent scripts, `make artifacts`)
| Stage | What it does |
|---|---|
| s00_download | Resumable streaming download of the UCSD `books`, `reviews_dedup`, `book_works`, `book_authors` and `book_genres_initial` files. No gunzip. |
| s01_books | One streaming pass over books JSON. Outputs `editions.parquet` (book_id→work_id, isbn, title, lang, image_url, url…), `descriptions.parquet`, `shelves_long.parquet` (work_id, shelf, count). |
| s02_meta | Works (best_book_id, original title/year), authors, UCSD coarse genre shares. Reuses the rating_dist parsing from old 00_prep. |
| s03_ratings | Streams reviews and maps book→**work** (collapses editions). Output: `ratings.parquet` (user, work, rating int8; 0 = read but unrated). **Swappable input.** |
| s04_catalog | Works with ≥20 distinct raters (a config value, confirmed by eval) and an English or unknown edition. Display edition, cover choice (skip `nophoto`), `series_key`/`series_pos` parsed from the title, box-set and children/comic flags. Expect about 70–100k works. |
| s05_matrix | `R_train.npz` (users with ≥3 catalog ratings × catalog). |
| s06_genres | Normalize shelves and remove non-genre ones (to-read, owned, kindle, years…). **LLM step:** send the top ~400 shelves to Claude (one-time, needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) to draft `shelf_genres.yaml` with display names and ~30 parent genres. The user reviews it, then per-work top-3 tags and a parent genre are computed with TF-IDF-damped weights. |
| s07_item_knn | Adjusted cosine with shrinkage `n_ij/(n_ij+λ)`, requiring n_ij≥5, computed in 1k-item blocks. Top-50 neighbors: `item_nbrs_idx.npy` (int32) and `item_nbrs_sim.npy` (f16). |
| s08_als | `implicit` ALS, 64 factors, graded confidence (5★>4★>3★>read; 1–2★ excluded). Outputs `item_factors.npy`, `yty.npy`, and L2-normalized `user_factors.npy` (f16, users with ≥10 ratings). If `implicit` won't install, fall back to a numpy CG-ALS. |
| s09_search_db | `catalog.db` (SQLite): works, FTS5 over title/author/series, and tables mapping edition→work, isbn→work and titlekey→work, plus a description snippet. |
| s10_package | `readers_csr.npz` (users × catalog, int8), `starter_shelf.json`, `manifest.json` (counts, params, sha256), sanity asserts. |

Artifacts total about 200–250 MB, and the server's memory use (RSS) should stay under about 500 MB. Load with `np.load(mmap_mode="r")`.

## Scoring (`core/scoring.py`, numpy only at serve time)
- **Fold-in:** a 64×64 solve for the user vector `u`, then `s_als = Y·u`. About 3 ms.
- **Item-item:** `S_ii(j) = Σ_i (r_i − b_u)·sim(i,j)` over the neighbor lists, with a shrunk user mean `b_u = (Σr + 3·5)/(n+5)`.
- **Blend** over the top 300 candidates from each model. When restrictive filters are active, score the whole catalog instead (still only a few ms) so filtered views don't run dry:
  `a(n)·z(s_als) + (1−a(n))·z(S_ii) + β·z(log pop) + γ·z(bayes_avg)`, with `a(n)=n/(n+k_a)`.
  - With few ratings the score leans on item-item; with many, on ALS.
  - With n=0, return the starter shelf.
- **Post-filters:**
  - Hide later series volumes, except "Next in series" when the user rated an earlier volume. Generalizes the old regexes in `recommender_classes.py` `find_neighbors`.
  - Hide box sets.
  - No per-author cap. Several books by the same author can appear.
  - Children's and comics off by default, with toggles.
  - User filters, applied after scoring and before truncating to `limit`, so a filtered list still returns a full page:
    - genre / parent genre;
    - author (typeahead, include or exclude);
    - publication year range;
    - minimum average rating;
    - minimum and maximum number of ratings (so users can seek hidden gems or proven favorites);
    - free-text search within results (title, author or tag).
- **Explanations:** "Because you liked X, Y" from the largest `w_i·sim(i,j)` terms.
- **Similar books:** item-item neighbors, padded with ALS cosine neighbors.
- **Similar readers** (`core/similar_readers.py`, shown when n ≥ 5):
  - Top 300 users by cosine in `user_factors`, then aggregate their rows in `readers_csr`.
  - **Popular:** similarity-weighted "% of similar readers read it", damped by global popularity.
  - **Top rated:** Bayesian neighbor average, requiring at least `max(5, M/100)` neighbor raters (the old `max(N/300,5)` idea).

## API (stateless; ratings live in browser localStorage)
- `GET /api/search?q=`: FTS5 prefix search ranked by bm25 and popularity. Returns work, title, author, year, cover, avg rating.
- `POST /api/import` (CSV) returns rated, read_unrated, to_read and unmatched lists plus stats.
  - Match order: Book Id→work, then ISBN13/ISBN (strip Excel's `="…"`), then normalized title plus author last name, with ties broken by ratings_count.
  - This extends `prep_data` in the old `recommender_classes.py`.
- `POST /api/recommend {ratings, read, dismissed, filters, limit, offset}` returns the lists below.
  - `filters`: `{genres[], authors_include[], authors_exclude[], year_min, year_max, min_avg_rating, min_ratings_count, max_ratings_count, text, include_children, include_comics, include_series_continuations}`.
  - Filters apply to every tab, including similar readers.
  - Scoring is cached per ratings hash in a small in-memory LRU, so changing filters only re-filters and doesn't re-score.
  - The response lists:  `for_you` (with `because`), `to_read_picks`, `similar_readers{popular, top_rated}|null`, `profile.top_genres` (you vs similar readers) and `meta`.
- `GET /api/books/{id}` (detail plus 20 similar), `/api/starter`, `/api/genres`, `/api/health`.
- `GET /api/authors?q=`: author typeahead for the filter (FTS5 over author names, ranked by total ratings).

## Frontend (React + Vite + TS)
- **Home:** two entry cards, Upload export and Rate books.
- **Rate:** debounced typeahead with a star widget on each result, an editable "Your shelf", and a starter grid of covers when empty. Recommendations refresh after each rating (debounced).
- **Results:**
  - Tabs: For You / Similar Readers: Popular / Similar Readers: Top Rated / From Your To-Read.
  - A filter bar shared across tabs:
    - genre chips;
    - author typeahead (include or exclude);
    - year range slider;
    - minimum average rating (star selector);
    - ratings-count range (log-scale slider, presets "Hidden gems" and "Popular");
    - search-within-results box;
    - children / comics / series toggles.
  - Filter state lives in the URL query string so views can be shared or bookmarked.
  - Cover-first cards with title, author, year, avg rating, genre tags, "Because you liked…", inline rating and dismiss.
  - A "your genres vs similar readers" profile chart.
- **Book modal:** description, tags, clickable similar-books strip.
- **Import summary:** match rate and unmatched list, with a note that the data ends in 2017.
- **Cover fallback chain:** Goodreads URL → Open Library by ISBN → a gradient placeholder colored by genre, showing title and author.

## Eval (`make eval`, uses the same `core.scoring` as the API)
- Hold out 10k test users with ≥10 ratings; they are excluded from s07 and s08 training.
- Hide 30% of each test user's ratings and fold in with visible ratings truncated to n ∈ {1,3,5,10,25,all}.
- Metrics: recall@20, NDCG@20, coverage, popularity bias, latency.
- Baselines: popularity, Bayesian top-rated, item-item only, ALS only.
- Grid over λ, K, factors/reg/α, k_a, β, γ. The chosen params go into `config/pipeline.yaml`, and the report goes to `eval/reports/`.

## Deployment
- Multi-stage Dockerfile: a node stage builds the frontend; a `python:3.12-slim` stage installs only the serving dependencies (fastapi, uvicorn, numpy, scipy, orjson, python-multipart) and bakes in the artifacts.
- Cloud Run: 1 vCPU, 1 GiB, min-instances 0.
- Artifacts are not committed. Publish them to GCS or a GitHub Release and add `make fetch-artifacts`.
- Add a Wan & McAuley citation in the footer (the data license is non-commercial).

## Build order
1. Scaffold (uv, Makefile, config), delete old files, move the fixture.
2. s00–s05.
3. s09 search, plus a minimal API and CLI to sanity-check matching.
4. s07, s08, core scoring.
5. Eval harness and tuning.
6. s06 genres (LLM draft, then user review).
7. Similar readers.
8. Full API.
9. Frontend.
10. Docker and deploy.
11. Rewrite CLAUDE.md.

## Verification
- s10 asserts: indices resolve, no NaNs, similarities in [−1,1], ≥95% of works have a genre tag, cover null rate reported.
- Unit tests (`uv run pytest`):
  - textnorm (series parse, ISBN cleanup, titlekey).
  - Fold-in matches `implicit.recalculate_user` within 1e-4.
  - Item-item scoring on a toy matrix.
  - Import of the fixture CSV gives a match rate of at least 85% for pre-2018 books.
  - Filters: each filter narrows results correctly, and a heavily filtered request still returns `limit` items when enough candidates exist.
- Persona smoke tests: Mistborn + Name of the Wind → fantasy-dominant; Gone Girl → thrillers; Sapiens → nonfiction.
- Eval gate: the blend beats item-item alone and ALS alone on NDCG@20 at n=3 and at n=all, and beats popularity at every n.
- Performance against the Docker image: search p95 under 30 ms, recommend p95 under 200 ms, import of 1k rows under 500 ms, RSS under 600 MB.
- Manual: `make serve` and try both flows in the browser (covers and fallbacks, re-rating, dismiss, tabs, book modal).

## Risks
- `implicit` wheels may be missing on arm64/py3.12; the fallback is a numpy ALS.
- 2017 cover URLs may be dead; the fallback chain covers this.
- Wrong `work_id` merges.
- Box sets polluting neighbor lists.
- A thin signal from 15M ratings; the fix is to swap in the interactions file at s03 if eval disappoints.

1. **Single-column ranked list:** every tab is now one column of full-width cards. The extra width fits a short description (about 3 lines) and up to 4 genre tags. Filters and the genre chart moved to a sticky right sidebar, so the list stays at the top. On phones the filters collapse behind a "Filters" button and the chart moves below the list.

Two things will look surprising at first, so the page now explains both:
- **Rank and predicted rating can disagree.** A book can rank #1 with a lower predicted rating than #5. The rank blends how well a book fits your taste with how likely you are to read it; the predicted rating is only the stars. A one-line note under the tabs says this.
- **Your sample export's predictions look low.** The Martian shows 3.7 against a 4.39 Goodreads average. You average 3.4 stars, about 0.7 below the typical rating for the same books, and 3 stars is your most common rating. So 3.7 means "better than usual for you." The page shows a note like this whenever someone's personal scale differs noticeably from the average.

## fe7c091a-020 · 2026-09-27 01:49 UTC

**Prompt**

> Awesome! Can you also add in the avg rating among similar readers for each book? And a way to sort by predicted score

**Claude**

Both features are in and live at http://localhost:8000. Refresh the Recommendations page to see them.

**Similar readers' average on every book.** Each card's score panel now shows three numbers, from most to least personal:
- your **predicted rating** (big);
- **Similar readers**: the average rating from your nearest readers, with how many of them rated it, e.g. ★ 4.1 (22). The count shows in italics when fewer than 3 rated it, so thin evidence is visible;
- the **Goodreads average**.

It appears in all four tabs. It shows "—" when none of your similar readers rated the book, and it only appears once you've rated at least 5 books, the same threshold as the readers-like-you tabs.

**Sort by predicted rating.** A "Sort by: Best match | Predicted rating" toggle sits above the list and works in every tab. The choice is saved in the URL, so a sorted view can be bookmarked. On the For you tab it re-sorts the whole pool of candidate books, not just the 40 loaded ones, so the best predictions rise even if they started far down: your top prediction goes from 3.8 in best-match order to 4.0–4.1. Books tied at the same displayed rating stay in best-match order. The explanation line under the tabs changes to describe the active sort.

**A bug the new sort exposed.** Sorting by prediction put *A Storm of Swords: Blood and Gold* at #1. That's a split edition of book 3 of A Song of Ice and Fire, which you haven't reached, so it should have been hidden. Titles ending in something like "#3: Part 2 of 2" weren't recognized as series books. I fixed that, which caught 76 more series titles and flagged 56 more collections and split editions (e.g. "#0.4, 0.5, 2.5") as box sets.

Rebuilding the catalog for that fix would have renumbered about 103,000 of the 105,000 books, because ties in the sort were ordered arbitrarily. That would have silently scrambled every recommendation. I kept the existing numbering, verified it matches exactly, and made the sort deterministic so future rebuilds are consistent.

All 17 tests pass, including new ones for the sort order and the similar-readers averages. The browser run showed no console errors on desktop or mobile, and the README and CLAUDE.md cover both features.

**Your books: new insights**

For your sample export, the three questions come out like this:

- **Books read:** 118 books puts you ahead of 95% of the 432,294 readers in the dataset. The typical reader has 5 and the top 10% have 61 or more. Take this one loosely: the dataset is Goodreads' *reviews* file, so other readers are counted by books they reviewed through 2017, which undercounts their reading. The page says so under the number.
- **Harshness:** you're harsher than 94% of the 159,734 readers with at least 10 ratings. You rate books 0.70★ below their average, while the typical reader rates 0.07★ above.
- **By genre:** you're tougher than Goodreads readers in every genre, most of all in Science & Nature (−1.12★) and Politics & Society (−0.99★), and least in Fantasy (−0.45★) and Science Fiction (−0.50★).

The genre table shows, per genre: how many books you've read and rated, your average, what all Goodreads readers gave those same books, the difference, and the typical rating across the whole genre. The first two insights appear as tiles with a percentile bar; your ratings chart is still there, with your average vs Goodreads' now in its caption.

These comparisons come from reader statistics precomputed from the full dataset, plus a new `/api/insights` endpoint. The harshness score compares each of your ratings with the book's average, the same baseline the predicted rating uses.

**About page: technical details**

There are 8 collapsed "Show technical details" toggles, each placed under the plain-language section it expands:

- **Similar books:** the similarity formula (adjusted cosine with shrinkage), neighbor-list size, how it's computed, and how your ratings vote.
- **Taste model:** the ALS settings, the confidence weights for each star level, how a new user is fitted without retraining, and how the settings were chosen.
- **Blend:** the scoring formula, how the model weight and popularity adjustment shift with your number of ratings, and the tuning results behind them.
- **Readers like you:** how nearest readers are found in taste space, and the formulas for the popular and top-rated lists.
- **Predicted rating:** the model's formula and an accuracy table showing error falling as you rate more (0.95★ at 1 rating to 0.86★ with a full history).
- **Data processing, evaluation protocol, and serving/architecture:** the rest of the pipeline end to end.

Every number comes from the actual configuration and measured runs.

One thing to know, which the evaluation details now state openly for a data science audience: the blend and ALS settings were tuned on subsamples of the same held-out users used for evaluation, so the reported accuracy is mildly optimistic. If you want a clean number, carving out a separate validation split and re-running the eval takes about 30 minutes, and I can do that next.

## fe7c091a-035 · 2026-09-27 03:54 UTC

**Prompt**

> what would I need to do to deploy this?

**Claude**

Most of the work is done: the app is already packaged as a Docker image (`Dockerfile`) that bakes in the frontend, the API and the ~311 MB of model/catalog files. What's left is getting that image built and hosted somewhere. I'd recommend **Google Cloud Run**; the app was designed with it in mind.

## Cloud Run steps

1. **Install and log in to Google Cloud's CLI:** `brew install --cask google-cloud-sdk`, then `gcloud auth login`. The login is interactive, so you have to do it yourself.
2. **Create a GCP project with billing enabled**, then turn on the services:
   `gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com cloudbuild.googleapis.com artifactregistry.googleapis.com`
3. **Build the image in the cloud.** You don't need Docker locally; Google's Cloud Build service builds it:
   ```bash
   gcloud artifacts repositories create goodrec --repository-format=docker --location=us-central1
   gcloud builds submit --tag us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/goodrec/app
   ```
4. **Deploy:**
   ```bash
   gcloud run deploy goodrec --image us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/goodrec/app \
     --region us-central1 --memory 1Gi --cpu 1 --allow-unauthenticated
   ```
   You get a public `https://goodrec-….run.app` URL.

## Things that would bite you

- **The data files aren't in Git.** `artifacts/` is gitignored and exists only on your laptop, so you must build from this machine or copy the folder wherever you build. Worse, Cloud Build skips gitignored files by default, so the image would come out with no data. You need a `.gcloudignore` file that includes `artifacts/`. I can add it.
- **The Dockerfile has never been built.** Docker isn't installed here, so the first Cloud Build run is its real test. I checked the pieces separately (the server imports with only its production dependencies, and the frontend builds), but expect a possible small fix on the first run.
- **Memory:** the server uses about 250 MB, so 1 GiB is the safe setting. The smallest tiers on free hosts (256–512 MB) are too tight.
- **Cold starts:** with Cloud Run's default of scaling to zero, the first visit after idle waits a few seconds while the container starts. Keeping one instance always on (`--min-instances 1`) avoids that for roughly $10–15/month. Otherwise light traffic should fit in the free tier plus a few cents a month to store the image. These are rough figures; check current GCP pricing.
- **About-page code links** point at `main`, so merge the branch first or they'll 404.

## Alternatives

- **Hugging Face Spaces (Docker):** likely free for a portfolio project. The free CPU tier has had plenty of memory for this app (about 16 GB last I knew; confirm current limits). You'd push the repo plus artifacts via Git LFS, and the Space sleeps when idle.
- **Fly.io or Render:** also fine with the same Dockerfile, but you'd need a paid plan with at least 1 GB of RAM.

If you want Cloud Run, I can now add the `.gcloudignore` and a `make deploy` target. Once you've installed and logged in to `gcloud`, send me your project ID and I'll run the build and deploy and fix anything the first build turns up.

**Claude**

For a portfolio demo, **probably yes, Hugging Face Spaces**, with one real tradeoff: cold starts.

**Why Spaces fits this project**
- **Cost and setup:** free, with no billing account or credit card. On Cloud Run you'd set up a billing account, the command-line tools and permissions, and pay roughly $10–15/month if you keep an instance warm.
- **Headroom:** the free CPU tier has historically offered far more memory than this app's ~250 MB (16 GB last I knew; worth confirming the current limits).
- **Simple deploys:** push a Git repo with the Dockerfile and it builds and runs. The 311 MB of data files go up with Git LFS, which Hugging Face handles fine.
- **Audience:** it's where people browse ML demos, and a Space page reads naturally as "here's my recommender" on a portfolio.

**Where Cloud Run is better**
- **Cold starts:** free Spaces go to sleep after a period with no visitors (around two days, as I recall), and the next visitor waits while it wakes, which can take a minute or more. Cloud Run's cold start is seconds, or zero with an always-on instance.
- **Polish and control:** custom domains, faster scaling, proper logs and monitoring. It looks more "production" if that's part of what you're showing.

**My take:** if the audience is people clicking a link from your GitHub or résumé, and an occasional slow first load is acceptable, go with Spaces: free and simple. If you'll send the link to recruiters and want it snappy every time, Cloud Run with one always-on instance is worth the ~$10–15/month.

**What Spaces would take on our side** (small):
1. Add a short config header to the Space's README pointing it at port 8080.
2. Keep GitHub as the main repo and push to a Hugging Face remote. The data files live only in the Space repo, via LFS, so GitHub stays lean.
3. Possibly run the container as a non-root user, which Hugging Face recommends. The app only reads files, so that's a one-line change.

Want me to set it up for Spaces? You'd create a free Hugging Face account and an empty Docker Space, send me its name, and give me a write token or push it yourself. I'll handle the rest.

## fe7c091a-037 · 2026-09-27 04:00 UTC

**Prompt**

> what about cloud run without an always-on instance?

**Claude**

That's probably the best option. It's nearly free, and cold starts are seconds rather than the minute-plus a sleeping Space takes.

**Cost:** close to $0 for portfolio traffic. With no always-on instance you're billed only while requests are being handled, and Cloud Run's monthly free allowance (on the order of hundreds of thousands of vCPU- and GiB-seconds; check current numbers) far exceeds what a demo uses. The only steady cost is storing the ~0.6 GB image, a few cents a month. You do still need a billing account with a card on file, so I'd set a budget alert at something like $5 for peace of mind.

**Cold start:** after roughly 15 minutes without traffic Cloud Run shuts the instance down, and the next visitor waits while a new one starts. For this app that's:
- starting the container (Cloud Run streams the image, so its size matters less than you'd think);
- loading Python, NumPy and SciPy, about a second or two;
- loading the artifacts, which takes about 0.4 s locally.

So I'd expect roughly **3–8 seconds** for that first visit, then the usual ~10–70 ms per request. The `--cpu-boost` flag gives the container extra CPU during startup and trims this further. That's an estimate, since we haven't run the image yet; I'd measure it after the first deploy.

**How it compares:**

| | Cold start | Cost | Setup |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cloud Run, scale to zero | ~3–8 s after idle (estimate) | ~free, card required | moderate |
| Cloud Run, 1 always-on instance | none | roughly $10–15/mo | moderate |
| HF Spaces (free) | a minute or more after it sleeps (~2 days idle) | free, no card | easy |

**My recommendation:** Cloud Run scaled to zero, with `--cpu-boost` and a budget alert. A few seconds' wait on the first click is fine for a portfolio link, it's effectively free, and you can add an always-on instance later with one command if it ever matters. Spaces only wins if you'd rather not put a card on file.

If you go this way, I'll add the `.gcloudignore` (so the data files get uploaded) and a `make deploy` target. You'd install `gcloud`, log in, create a project with billing enabled, and send me the project ID, and I'll run the first build and deploy.

**Claude**

The predicted score now shows 2 decimals and is calibrated to your own rating distribution. It's running locally at http://localhost:8000; all 28 tests pass, and the browser check showed no errors. It isn't committed or deployed yet.

**What changed for your shelf:**

| Your top 40 | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Best match: predicted 4.0+ | 1 | 13 |
| Best match: predicted 4.5+ | 0 | 7 |
| Sort by predicted: range | 3.6–4.0 | 4.77–4.81 |
| Anything at 4.9+ | 0 | 0 |

**How it works:**
1. The model's raw prediction is lined up, percentile for percentile, against the ratings you've actually given. Your top ~15–18% of predictions land between 4.5 and 5.0, the way your 5★ ratings do.
2. Near the top, predictions approach 5 without ever reaching it, so nothing piles up at the ceiling.
3. With only a handful of ratings, your distribution is blended with the dataset-wide one, and it leans on yours more as you rate more. Below 5 ratings you see the raw number.
4. Calibration only changes the displayed number, never an ordering, so both rankings are unchanged.

On 1,200 held-out users, 29% of calibrated predictions are 4.5+ against 33% actual 5★, and 9.6% fall below 2.5 against 9.4% actual 1–2★. The cost is accuracy: the typical miss grows from 0.86 to 0.99 stars. That's the price of predictions that look like your ratings instead of hugging your average. The About page explains this, with the formula and these numbers in the technical details.

**Two things you'll notice:**
- **Some top recommendations now show low predictions.** For example, #3 *Guns, Germs, and Steel* shows 2.42 (raw 3.23). The model always thought you'd rate these below your average; calibration just makes it visible. They rank high because Best match also weighs what readers like you read, not only predicted stars. If that feels off, I could have the ranking account for predicted rating more, or drop recommendations predicted well below your average.
- **Predicted-sort values cluster tightly** (4.77–4.81). Those books all score above everything you've rated, so they're in the zone that approaches 5 gradually. I can widen that zone to spread them out more, at the cost of letting a few get closer to 5.00.

<details><summary>Claude's plan (approved)</summary>

# Plan: Predicted-rating floor for For you

## Context
Since calibration made predictions spread out, some of the top For you picks show low predicted ratings. For the sample shelf, 13 of the top 40 are below 3.0, e.g. #3 at 2.42. Best match ranks on the blend of similar books, taste model and popularity, and ignores the predicted rating. The user wants the ranking to account for it more, and left the implementation to me.

**Scope decision:** no ubiquity or popularity correction in the readers-like-you lists. The user's view: if a book is extremely popular with readers like them, that's a useful signal. For you's popularity handling is also left unchanged.

**Read-only experiments already run** (800 held-out users, NDCG@20):

| Option | NDCG n=3 | n=10 | full history | Sample shelf, top 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Current | .0604 | .0963 | .1367 | 13 below 3.0, min 1.27 |
| Floor at user's average | .0604 | .0875 | .1294 (−5%) | 0 below 3.0, min 3.45; 27 at ≥ 4 |
| Floor at average − 0.5 | .0604 | .0923 | .1340 (−2%) | 1 below 3.0, min 2.94 |
| Weight δ = 0.5 on z(pred) | .0575 | .0930 | .1293 (−5%) | 4 below 3.0 |
| Weight δ = 1.0 on z(pred) | .0561 | .0877 | .1182 (−14%) | 1 below 3.0 |

- A floor beats adding a weight, and a small weight on top of the floor doesn't help.
- NDCG measures whether a user *reads and loves* a book, while the predicted rating estimates how much they'd like it *if* they read it. So some cost is expected: this trades a little accuracy for recommendations that match their own predicted ratings.

## Changes

### 1. Prediction floor for For you (`src/goodrec/core/scoring.py`)
- **New helper:** `prediction_floor(user, raw_pred, cal, offset) -> bool mask`.
  - It keeps books whose calibrated prediction (`apply_calibration`) is at least the user's average rating minus `offset`.
  - It applies only when calibration exists (≥ 5 ratings); otherwise it keeps everything, so new users are unchanged.
- **In `ranking()`:**
  - Compute `preds_all` for the whole base universe for both sorts. Today this only happens for the predicted sort; the vectorized `predict_ratings` takes about 60 ms and is cached on `raw.cache`.
  - Apply the floor to `base` before `_pool()`, so the candidate pool refills with books above the floor.
  - Stable ranks keep working unchanged, because the floor is part of the unfiltered universe.
- **Calibration input:** `ranking()` and `recommend()` take a `prior` argument (dataset rating distribution). `api/main.py` passes `state["population"]["rating_dist"]`, and the calibration is shared via `raw.cache["calib"]`, the same cache `_shown()` uses.
- **Scope:** For you only.
  - To-read picks are unaffected (it's the user's own list).
  - Popular and Top rated are unaffected (they mean "what readers like you read or rated").
  - Explore and search are unaffected.
- **Config:** `blend.pred_floor_offset` in `config/pipeline.yaml`.
  - Measure offsets 0 and 0.25 on 1,200 held-out users.
  - Default to **0.0** (floor at the user's average), unless the full-history NDCG cost exceeds ~6%; if so, use 0.25.
  - The user-facing rule: "We don't recommend books we predict you'd rate below your average."

### 2. Eval and docs
- **`src/goodrec/eval/run.py`:** add a "blend + prediction floor" row to the report, using the shared `prediction_floor()` and `calibration()` helpers, so the tradeoff stays measured.
- **About page** (`frontend/src/pages/AboutPage.tsx`):
  - One sentence in the plain-language Blend section.
  - The floor rule plus its measured NDCG cost in the Blend technical details.
  - A code link for `prediction_floor()`: add it to `LINKS` in `scripts/code_links.py` and regenerate.
- **README / CLAUDE.md:** one line each.

## Critical files
- `src/goodrec/core/scoring.py`: `ranking()`, the new `prediction_floor()`, `recommend()` signature.
- `src/goodrec/api/main.py`: pass `prior` to `recommend()` and `ranking()`.
- `config/pipeline.yaml`: `blend.pred_floor_offset`.
- `src/goodrec/eval/run.py`, `frontend/src/pages/AboutPage.tsx`, `scripts/code_links.py`, `tests/test_api.py`.

## Verification
1. **Tests** (`PYTHONPATH=src uv run pytest -q`). All 28 existing tests, especially stable ranks and sort-by-predicted, plus new ones:
   - For a user with ≥ 5 ratings, no For you book's `predicted_rating` is below their average minus the offset.
   - With < 5 ratings, the For you list is identical to before.
   - Ranks stay stable under filters with the floor on.
2. **Offline:** held-out NDCG for the floor offsets (1,200 users). Record the chosen default in `config/pipeline.yaml`.
3. **Before/after, sample shelf top 40:** count below 3.0, count at ≥ 4 and at ≥ 4.5, lowest prediction.
4. **Browser (Playwright, as before):** For you shows no low predictions; stable ranks, filters, sort by predicted, and map view still work; no console errors.
5. **Report** the NDCG cost and the before/after counts. Don't commit or deploy unless asked.

</details>

- **See your reading life:** every rated book grouped by stars, your to-read list, your Goodreads reviews, and books from your export that aren't in the catalog (mostly post-2017 reads).
- **Use the recommender:** it looks up your For you list with any filters, "readers like you", catalog search, book details (your predicted rating, similar books, how similar readers rated it), your shelves and your reviews. Ranks and predicted ratings match the rest of the app.
- **Go beyond 2017:** it uses its own knowledge plus Claude's web search, and says when a book is from outside the catalog.
- **Book-club talk:** a "Chat about this book →" link in every book pop-up starts a conversation about that book.
- **Starter buttons:** What should I read next? · Find me something specific… · Great books since 2017 for me · Pick from my to-read list · What does my reading say about me? · Talk about a book I've read · More like a book I loved · Take me outside my comfort zone. The three that end in "…", "a book I've read" and "a book I loved" fill in the start of a prompt for you to finish.

**Limits on your API spend:** 40 messages per visitor per day, 1,500 messages per day across everyone, and 30 messages per conversation. They're in `config/pipeline.yaml` under `chat:`. The counters live in each server's memory, so they reset on restart and aren't shared between Cloud Run instances.

**Two things I couldn't check without a key:**
- Whether Claude actually uses the tools well on your two example questions.
- The web search setting. I used `web_search_20250305`, the tool version I know. If Anthropic has a newer one it's a one-line config change, but I haven't confirmed which is current.

**Also changed:**
- Imports now keep review text and the books that couldn't be matched. **You'll need to re-import your Goodreads CSV** for Ask to see your reviews and post-2017 reads.
- `anthropic` is now a server dependency.
- README, CLAUDE.md and the About page have a new Ask section, and the privacy note says ratings and reviews go to Anthropic when you chat.

Nothing is committed or deployed.

**To deploy it:**

<details><summary>Claude's plan (approved)</summary>

# Plan: "Ask" chat tab — a reading assistant that knows your shelf

## Context
The user wants a chatbot tab that:
- gives specialized recommendations ("a nonfiction book about the history of science");
- can see their whole reading life: ratings, reviews, to-read list, For you picks and books from similar readers;
- can recommend books outside the 2017 dataset;
- can talk about books like a book-club buddy.

Starter buttons should show what it's good at.

**Decisions (from the user):**
- The server uses the owner's Anthropic key, with guardrails.
- The model is **Sonnet 5** (`claude-sonnet-5`).
- Claude's **web search tool** is enabled for post-2017 books.

**Approach.** Claude runs a tool-use loop on the server. The tools wrap the functions the API already has, so the recommender still does the ranking and Claude supplies judgment, conversation and outside knowledge:
- `recommend()` with `_filters()`
- the readers-like-you lists
- `Catalog.search`
- `detail` and `similar_books`
- personal predictions

The API stays stateless. The browser sends the shelf and the transcript on each turn, like `/api/recommend`.

## 1. Data the chat needs that we don't keep yet
- **`api/matching.py` `parse_export`:**
  - Also return each row's `My Review`, trimmed to about 1,500 characters and with HTML stripped.
  - Also return the rating and shelf for **unmatched** rows. These are mostly post-2017 reads, which are exactly the signal needed for "new books for me".
- **`/api/import`:** pass both through.
- **`frontend/src/store.tsx`:** add two fields, kept on re-import with the same replace logic as ratings:
  - `reviews: Record<id, string>`
  - `outside: {title, author, rating, shelf}[]`
  - Cap the total at about 1 MB, which is safe for localStorage.

## 2. Backend: `src/goodrec/api/chat.py` (new FastAPI router, mounted in `main.py`)
- **Refactor first:** move the body of `recommend_route` into `_recommend_payload(req)` in `main.py`. The route and the chat tools then share it, so ranks, calibration, the YA default and the prediction floor stay identical.
- **`POST /api/chat`:**
  - Request body: `{messages, shelf: {ratings, read, to_read, dismissed, reviews, outside}}`.
  - Response: an **SSE stream** of events:
    - `text` deltas
    - `status`, e.g. "Checking your recommendations…" or "Searching the web…"
    - `books`: catalog book payloads the reply mentions, so the UI can render covers
    - `done` or `error`
- **Loop:**
  - Use `anthropic.Anthropic().messages.stream(...)` with the tools below.
  - Run our tools locally and send back the `tool_result`s.
  - Handle `pause_turn` for the server-side web search.
  - Stop after 6 tool rounds.
- **System prompt:** built per request, marked with `cache_control` so follow-up turns in a conversation are cheap. It contains:
  - The role: a warm, candid book-club friend who knows this reader's taste.
  - Honesty rules:
    - Only call a book "in your recommendations" if a tool returned it.
    - Say when a book is post-2017 or outside the dataset.
    - Don't invent predicted ratings.
    - Reference catalog books as `[[book:<work_id>]]`, which the UI renders as cards.
  - A **library digest**:
    - Every rated book as a compact `title — author (year) ★n` line, grouped by stars. About 15 tokens per book, so 1,000 books is roughly 15k tokens, which caching makes affordable.
    - To-read titles.
    - Outside-the-dataset reads.
    - Insights: harshness, genre mix, average rating (reuse the `/api/insights` logic).
    - Which books have reviews.
    - For very large libraries (more than 2,500 books): 4–5★ and 1–2★ books in full, plus counts for the rest.
- **Tools** (read-only, JSON-schema'd, each returns compact JSON with `work_id`s):

  | Tool | Wraps |
  |---|---|
  | `get_recommendations(genres?, tags?, text?, year_min/max?, min_avg_rating?, include_ya?, sort?, limit≤20)` | `_recommend_payload` For you |
  | `readers_like_you(kind: popular\|top_rated, …same filters)` | readers lists |
  | `search_catalog(query, limit≤10)` | `Catalog.search`, annotated with read / rated / to-read and your predicted rating |
  | `book_details(work_id)` | `detail`, `/books/{id}/personal` logic (predicted rating, similar readers' average, "because you liked"), top 8 `similar_books` |
  | `my_library(shelf: rated\|to_read\|read, min_rating?, genre?, text?, limit)` | the shelf the client sent, joined to the catalog |
  | `my_review(work_id)` | full review text from the client-sent shelf |
  | `list_genres_and_tags()` | so Claude maps "history of science" onto real tags (e.g. `History`, `Science & Nature`) |
  | `web_search` (Anthropic server tool, `max_uses: 3` per turn) | post-2017 books, reviews, author news |
- **Guardrails** (constants in `config/pipeline.yaml` under `chat:`):
  - 40 messages per visitor per day, keyed by the `X-Forwarded-For` IP with an in-memory counter per instance.
  - 30 turns per conversation.
  - A global daily message cap.
  - `max_tokens` 1,500.
  - Request body up to 2 MB.
  - Return a friendly 429 message when a cap is hit.
  - Hard backstop: a monthly spend limit set in the Anthropic console (manual step, documented in the README).
- **Key handling:**
  - Locally: read `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment.
  - Cloud Run: store it in **Secret Manager** (`gcloud secrets create anthropic-key`) and add `--set-secrets ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=anthropic-key:latest` to `make deploy`.
  - Without a key, `/api/chat` returns 503 and the tab shows "Chat isn't configured".
- **Dependencies:** move `anthropic` from the pipeline-only group to the main dependencies (`pyproject.toml`), so the Docker image includes it.

## 3. Frontend: `frontend/src/pages/ChatPage.tsx`, nav tab "Ask"
- **Tab:** placed after Your books. Uses the URL view `chat`. Lazy-loaded like the About page.
- **Empty state:** a short intro plus **starter buttons**, each sending (or prefilling) a prompt:
  1. **What should I read next?** A mix of For you, similar readers and your to-read list, with reasons.
  2. **Find me something specific…** Prefills "I'm in the mood for " so the user finishes the sentence.
  3. **Great books since 2017 for my taste.** Uses the web search.
  4. **Pick from my to-read list.** Ranks your to-read books by fit and mood.
  5. **What does my reading say about me?** A taste profile, blind spots and patterns.
  6. **Talk about a book I've read.** Book-club mode: themes, questions, what to read after.
  7. **Take me outside my comfort zone.** Well-matched books from genres you rarely read.
- **Conversation:**
  - Streaming messages rendered as markdown. Use a small renderer such as `marked`, or plain paragraphs plus lists to avoid a dependency.
  - `[[book:id]]` markers become inline mini cards that open the existing book pop-up (`onOpen`).
  - Status lines while tools run.
  - A "New chat" button.
- **Storage:** the transcript is kept in localStorage (`goodrec.chat.v1`), so it survives reloads.
- **Book pop-up:** add a **"Chat about this book"** button that opens Ask with "Let's talk about *Title*".
- **Empty shelf:** if the user hasn't rated anything, the tab still works for general book talk, and it nudges them to import or rate for personalization.
- **Privacy:** a one-line note that ratings and reviews are sent to Anthropic when you chat. Also add it to the About page.
- **Plumbing:** `api.ts` gets `chatStream(messages, shelf, onEvent)` using `fetch` plus a `ReadableStream` SSE parser.

## Critical files
- **New:** `src/goodrec/api/chat.py`, `frontend/src/pages/ChatPage.tsx`, `tests/test_chat.py`.
- **Modified:**
  - `src/goodrec/api/main.py` (the `_recommend_payload` refactor, router mount)
  - `api/matching.py`, `api/schemas.py`
  - `frontend/src/store.tsx`, `api.ts`, `App.tsx` (tab), `useUrlState.ts` (view), the book pop-up component
  - `styles.css`
  - `config/pipeline.yaml` (`chat:` caps)
  - `pyproject.toml`, `Makefile` (deploy secrets)
  - `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `AboutPage.tsx`

## Verification
1. **Unit tests, no API calls:**
   - Each tool function returns correct, filter-respecting data. For example, `get_recommendations(tags=["History of Science"])` returns only matching books with the same ranks as `/api/recommend`.
   - `my_review` returns the review text.
   - Import keeps reviews and outside books.
   - Caps return 429.
   - Missing key returns 503.
   - The stream is tested with a fake Anthropic client that emits a tool call, then text.
2. **Live smoke script** (local, real key): run the user's two example prompts and each starter button on the sample export. Check:
   - Catalog picks are real `work_id`s and aren't already read.
   - The post-2017 answer uses web search and names books that aren't in the catalog.
   - Book-club follow-ups stay on topic.
   - Log tokens and cost per conversation.
3. **Browser (Playwright):**
   - Starter buttons work.
   - Streaming renders.
   - Book cards open the pop-up.
   - The transcript persists after a reload.
   - Mobile layout works.
   - No console errors.
4. Full pytest suite and a frontend build.
5. Don't commit or deploy unless asked. Deploying also requires the Secret Manager step, which I'll walk through.

**Claude**

The blank replies are fixed, and I confirmed it against the real API with your key (a few cents of usage). All 38 tests pass. Your running server has already reloaded, so click **New chat** to clear the blank bubbles, which were saved, and try again.

**Cause:** Sonnet 5 thinks before it answers. The reply was capped at 1,500 tokens, and on the newer-books question the thinking used all of it, so the answer never started. "hi" worked because it needed almost no thinking.

**Fixes:**
- **Bigger reply budget:** raised to 16,000 tokens, which covers thinking plus the answer.
- **Effort setting:** a new `effort: medium` option in `config/pipeline.yaml`. Set it to `low` for faster replies or `high` for more careful ones.
- **"Thinking…" status** now shows while the model thinks.
- **No more silent blanks:** if a reply ever ends with no text, you get an error message and your question goes back in the box, instead of an empty bubble.

**How the real answers looked:**
- **"Books published since 2017":** it ran two web searches, then recommended books like *Alien Clay* (Tchaikovsky) and *The Mountain in the Sea* (Nayler). Each tied to specific books you rated, such as *Children of Time* and *Other Minds*. It took about 45 seconds.
- **History of science:** it used your recommendations plus catalog search and suggested *A Short History of Nearly Everything* (your #4), *The Code Book*, *The Ancestor's Tale* and more, each with its predicted rating. It took about 15 seconds.

**Found while testing:** in one run it said you'd rated *The Emperor of All Maladies* 3★. That book is actually on your to-read list, unrated. I changed two things so this is less likely:
- Catalog search now lists books you've read separately, so they can't be recommended back to you.
- The instructions tell it that "on to-read shelf" means unread, and to say when a pick is already on your to-read list.

**Speed and usage:** each message sends your library summary (about 25k tokens). It's cached after the first message, so follow-ups in the same chat are cheaper. Web-search questions are the slow ones. If they feel too slow, switching `effort` to `low` is the easiest lever.

## fe7c091a-058 · 2026-09-27 18:25 UTC

**Prompt**

> help me ballpark the cost (in dollars) of a cheap and an expensive request just so I know how much to keep in my balance

**Claude**

These estimates use the token counts from the real test requests I just ran, but the prices are assumed. I'm using Sonnet 4.x pricing because I haven't confirmed Sonnet 5's. Check anthropic.com/pricing and scale if it differs.

| Assumed price | Per million tokens |
|---|---|
| Input | $3 |
| Output (includes thinking) | $15 |
| Cache write | $3.75 |
| Cache read | $0.30 |
| Web search | $10 per 1,000 searches (1¢ each) |

**Per message:**

| Request | What it used | ≈ Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Follow-up chat ("hi", a quick question) in an active conversation | ~25k cached library tokens read, ~100–300 output | **~1¢** |
| First message of a new chat (writes your ~25k-token library to the cache) | +25k cache write | **~10¢** |
| Catalog question (history of science: 2 tool calls) | ~800 output, ~25k read, 3k–28k written | **4–13¢** |
| Web-search question (books since 2017: 2 searches, long thinking) | ~3,200 output, ~45k written, 2 searches | **~25–35¢** |
| Absolute worst case per message (all 16k output tokens, 3 searches, cold cache) | | **~50¢** |

**Rules of thumb:**
- A typical conversation of 5–10 messages costs about **20–60¢**. One dominated by web searches is closer to $1–2.
- The cache expires after about 5 minutes of inactivity, so the next message after a pause pays the ~10¢ first-message cost again.
- A bigger Goodreads library means a bigger library summary, so every message costs more. The cost grows roughly in proportion to the number of books.

**How much to keep in your balance:**
- **Just you testing:** $10 lasts a long time (100+ messages).
- **Public site:** the current caps could in theory reach about **$150–200/day**: 1,500 messages a day at a 10–15¢ average. That's too loose for a portfolio project. I'd suggest two things:
  - Lower `global_daily` in `config/pipeline.yaml` from 1500 to about **150**, which caps worst-case spend at roughly $15–25/day.
  - Set a monthly spend limit in the Anthropic console (**Settings → Limits**), e.g. $20. That's the hard stop no matter what the app does.

Want me to lower the global cap to 150?

**Claude**

Yes. **Haiku 4.5** (`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`) is Anthropic's cheapest current model: about **$1 input / $5 output per million tokens**, roughly a third of the Sonnet prices I assumed. One correction to my wording: the app runs **Sonnet 5**. "Sonnet 4.x" was only the pricing I borrowed because I haven't confirmed Sonnet 5's.

At Haiku prices, the same requests would cost about:

| Request | Sonnet (est.) | Haiku 4.5 |
|---|---|---|
| Follow-up in an active chat | ~1¢ | ~0.3¢ |
| First message of a chat | ~10¢ | ~3¢ |
| Catalog question | 4–13¢ | 1–4¢ |
| Web-search question | 25–35¢ | ~10¢ (searches stay 1¢ each) |

**What you'd give up:**
- **Book knowledge:** thinner, especially for less famous and newer books. That matters most for "Help me find newer books", where Haiku leans harder on web search.
- **Book-club conversation:** less insightful about themes and less nuanced about your taste.
- **Following instructions:** somewhat more likely to make mistakes like the "you rated it 3★" slip, even though the tools still do the ranking.

**Other ways to cut cost while keeping Sonnet:**
- **Smaller library summary:** this is the biggest cost driver. The ~25k-token summary is re-cached every new chat. Listing only 4–5★ and 1–2★ books, with counts for the rest, could roughly halve the per-message cost.
- **Lower `effort`:** `low` means less thinking, so fewer output tokens and faster replies.
- **Lower `global_daily`:** this caps the worst case on the public site.

Switching models is a one-line change: `chat.model` in `config/pipeline.yaml`. Before you decide, I could run your two example questions on Haiku and show you the answers next to Sonnet's, for a few cents. Want me to?

**Why it was #384:** its 4.80 predicted rating mostly reflects that it's a very highly rated book, adjusted for how you rate. The taste model scores it well below average for you. None of your rated books are close neighbors of it, and **none of your 300 most similar readers has read it**. So similar-reader overlap couldn't have helped. **The fix:** Best match adds a boost for high predicted ratings, weighted by fame (Goodreads ratings count). The weight is zero at 10k ratings and full at about 316k.

| *The Woman from Tantoura* / *The Harafish* (obscure) | ~#400 / #382 | unchanged |

The average predicted rating of your top 40 rose from 4.05 to 4.40, and *The Way of Kings*, *Flowers for Algernon* and *Unbroken* are now in your top 10.

**Cost:** measured on 993 held-out users, it lowers accuracy (NDCG@20) about 5.6% for full histories and about 2% with 10 ratings. The same boost without the fame weighting cost about 14%.

## fe7c091a-065 · 2026-09-27 19:21 UTC

**Prompt**

> explain the taste model for me

**Claude**

The **taste model** is the part of the recommender that learns patterns in *who reads what* across all 465,000 readers in the dataset. The other part, "similar books", only looks at books directly related to ones you've rated.

**What it learns.** The model is trained on 15.7 million ratings and places every reader and every book at a point in a shared "taste space" with 64 hidden dimensions. Nobody labels these dimensions; they come out of the data. In practice they tend to capture things like "hard sci-fi vs. space opera", "literary vs. commercial", "narrative history", "romance-adjacent" and "reads what's on bestseller lists". Two books end up close together when the same kinds of people read them, even if they never share a reader directly.

A book's score for you is how closely your point lines up with its point (a dot product). A high score means "people shaped like you read this."

**How your ratings feed it.** It's a method called *implicit-feedback ALS*. It treats each book you've shelved as a signal that you're drawn to it, weighted by how strongly:

| Your shelf | Weight |
|---|---|
| 5★ | 31 |
| 4★ | 22 |
| 3★ | 10 |
| Read, not rated | 7 |
| 1–2★ | not counted as interest |
| Everything else | 1: a weak "probably not interested" |

So it isn't trying to predict your star rating. It predicts **what you'd pick up and like**, based on everything you've chosen to read. A 2★ book doesn't count as a sign you'd like similar books, but it doesn't count against them either.

**New users.** Book positions are learned offline once. When you import or rate books, the server solves for your position using your weighted shelf and the fixed book positions (called "fold-in"). That's one small calculation, under a millisecond, so your recommendations update instantly as you rate.

**How much it counts.** In Best match, the taste model's weight is `a = n / (n + 20)`, where n is your number of ratings. With 3 ratings it gets 13% and similar books dominate. With your 117 it gets about 85%, so it's the main driver of your ranking. It's also the basis of "readers like you": those are the 300 readers whose points are closest to yours in the same space.

**Good at:**
- Picking up broad taste from many books, like "you read big-idea science nonfiction and cerebral sci-fi", and finding books in that neighborhood you haven't touched. That's why *A Short History of Nearly Everything* ranks high for you even though no single book you rated is its close neighbor.

**Blind spots:**
- **What you'd pick up, not how much you'd like it.** It predicts reading behavior, not enjoyment. That's why *The Green Mile* scored low: the people who read it sit in a different region of the space than the people who read your books (none of your 300 nearest readers had read it). Your predicted rating is a separate model: the book's average, adjusted for how you rate, plus similar books you've rated. It says you'd probably love the book if you picked it up. The new fame-gated boost is how the two now get reconciled.
- **Rare books:** it has little to go on for books with few readers.
- **Nuance within a genre:** its 64 dimensions capture broad strokes, not why you loved one thriller and hated another.

The code is `train_als()` in `s08_als.py` for training and `fold_in()` in `core/scoring.py` for placing you, both linked from the About page's technical details.

## fe7c091a-066 · 2026-09-27 19:23 UTC

**Prompt**

> and explain the fame-gated boosting for me please

**Claude**

**The problem it solves.** Your Best match ranking came almost entirely from two signals: the taste model ("people like you read this") and similar books ("this sits next to books you rated highly"). Your **predicted rating** ("how many stars would you give it?") had no say in the order. So a book you'd probably love could sit at #384 just because readers like you hadn't happened to read it. The boost gives the predicted rating a say.

**Why it's "fame-gated."** The predicted rating starts from the book's average rating, adjusts it for how harshly or generously you rate, and then corrects it using similar books you've rated. For a book with no connection to anything you've read, that last correction is close to zero, so the prediction is mostly "this book has a high average." Many obscure books have very high averages because only devoted fans rate them: *The Woman from Tantoura* is predicted at 4.76, almost the same as *The Green Mile*. An unrestricted boost would flood your list with niche books you've never heard of. So the boost is scaled by how well known the book is:

| Goodreads ratings | Fame weight |
|---|---|
| 10,000 or fewer | 0 |
| 31,000 | 0.33 |
| 100,000 | 0.67 |
| ~316,000 or more | 1 (full boost) |

It's measured on a log scale, so going from 10k to 100k counts as much as going from 100k to 1M. The reasoning: a famous book with a high average has been rated by a broad audience, so its high prediction is trustworthy. A niche book's high average may reflect only its biggest fans.

**The formula.** Each book's Best match score gets one extra term:

**boost = a(n) × 0.75 × fame × z(predicted rating)**

- **z(predicted rating):** how far above or below the other candidates the book's prediction is, in standard deviations.
- **0.75:** the overall strength, `delta_pred` in the config.
- **a(n) = n/(n+20):** shrinks the boost for users with few ratings, whose predictions are less reliable. With your 117 ratings, a = 0.85.

**Your numbers.** For scale, your #1 book scores 3.68 and your #40 scores 1.37.

| Book | Goodreads ratings | Fame | Predicted | Boost | New rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *The Count of Monte Cristo* | 612k | 1.00 | 4.73 | +1.52 | #42 → **#9** |
| *Lonesome Dove* | 118k | 0.72 | 4.79 | +1.30 | #176 → **#40** |
| *The Green Mile* | 195k | 0.86 | 4.80 | **+1.69** | #384 → **#96** |
| *Hamilton: The Revolution* | 28k | 0.29 | 4.77 | +0.48 | #256 → #142 |
| *The Woman from Tantoura* | 16k | 0.14 | 4.76 | +0.22 | ~#400 → #394 |

*The Green Mile* gets the biggest boost of the five, but it started so far down (the taste model scores it below average for you) that it only reaches #96.

**One more piece:** the recommender only ranks a candidate pool of about 400–600 books, made from each model's top 300. The 50 books with the highest fame-weighted predictions are now also added to that pool, so a famous book you'd likely love can't be missed just because neither model shortlisted it.

**The tradeoff.** On 993 held-out users, the boost lowers the recommender's accuracy score (NDCG@20: how well the top 20 contain books people actually went on to read and love) by about 5.6% for full histories and about 2% with 10 ratings. Without the fame gate, the same boost cost about 14%. Some cost is expected, because the boost values "you'd rate it highly" over "you'd likely pick it up".

**Where it doesn't apply:** the Popular and Top rated lists from readers like you, and "Sort by predicted rating", which already orders purely by prediction.

*Gone with the Wind* ranks low for the same reason *The Green Mile* did. It's popular and has a high predicted rating, but **none of your 300 most similar readers has read it**, so the recommender's main signal counts against it.

One caveat first: on the sample library (`tests/fixtures/goodreads_library_export.csv`) it ranks #225, not #106. The shelf saved in your browser must differ a bit from that file, for example books you've rated on the site since importing. I can't see your browser's shelf, so the numbers below are from the sample, but the pattern should be the same.

**How its score is built**, compared with books that rank well:

| Book | Rank | Predicted | Taste model | Popularity | Prediction boost | **Total** | Similar readers who read it |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *The Martian* | #1 | 4.58 | +2.57 | −0.62 | +0.90 | **+3.68** | 108 of 300 (avg 4.24★) |
| *Monte Cristo* | #9 | 4.73 | +1.15 | −0.29 | +1.52 | **+2.56** | 11 (avg 4.36★) |
| *The Green Mile* | #96 | 4.80 | −0.98 | −0.10 | +1.69 | **+0.57** | 0 |
| *Gone with the Wind* | #225 | 4.65 | **−1.11** | −0.30 | +1.23 | **−0.12** | **0** |

Similar books adds almost nothing for any of these (−0.03 to +0.19, and +0.05 for *Gone with the Wind*), so I've left it out.

For scale, #40 scores about +1.37 and #100 about +0.56.

What's pulling it down:

1. **Your similar readers haven't read it.** The 300 readers closest to your taste lean heavily toward sci-fi, science and narrative nonfiction: 108 of them read *The Martian*. Not one read *Gone with the Wind*. The people who read it sit elsewhere in the dataset, closer to historical fiction, romance and classics readers. That's why the taste model scores it well below the other candidates (−1.11). It's still in the top 13% of all your unread books, but the other candidates are ranked higher.
2. **The high prediction rests on thin evidence about you.** The 4.65 comes mostly from the book's high average, adjusted for how you rate. Of its close neighbors, you've rated only one: *East of Eden* (5★), which nudges it up.
3. **Popularity counts slightly against it.** For long reading histories, the recommender dials popularity down a little (−0.30), so heavy readers don't just get bestsellers.

The fame-gated boost is working as intended: it gives the book the full +1.23, which moves it from about #400 to #225 on the sample. But it's pushing against a strong "not your usual read" signal.

**What we could do:**
- **Leave it.** This is the ranking doing its job: Best match means "what readers like you gravitate toward," and **Sort by predicted rating** already gives the "books I'd most likely love" view, where *Gone with the Wind* ranks near the top.
- **Turn the boost up:** strength 1.0 would lift it modestly, at about an 8% accuracy cost. It would still land outside the top 100.
- **Let a very high prediction partly override the taste model** for famous books. That's a bigger change to what Best match means, and it would cost more accuracy.

I'd leave it and use Sort by predicted rating for this kind of book. Want me to try either change?

## fe7c091a-069 · 2026-09-27 20:04 UTC

**Prompt**

> Curious why Magic Mountain gets a prediction of 2.82, Doctor Faustus gets 3.26, and Buddenbrooks gets 4.28. In reality, I've ready Magic Mountain and gave it 5 stars but it's interesting Buddenbrooks would be predicted to be so much higher

**Claude**

The short answer: for these three books, the recommender has **no personal evidence at all**, and calibration exaggerates a small, noisy difference between them. The numbers below are from the sample library, where they show 2.64, 2.67 and 3.89. The shelf in your browser gives slightly different values (2.82, 3.26, 4.28), but the mechanism is the same.

**How each prediction is built:**

| | Book average in the dataset | + Your harshness | + Correction from related books you rated | = Raw | → Shown |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *The Magic Mountain* | 3.96 | −0.67 | +0.01 | 3.29 | **2.64** |
| *Doctor Faustus* | 3.97 | −0.67 | +0.00 | 3.30 | **2.67** |
| *Buddenbrooks* | 4.21 | −0.67 | +0.01 | 3.54 | **3.89** |

1. **Nothing you've rated is connected to Mann.** The correction step is zero. The only link found is *The Brothers Karamazov*, and it's negligible (similarity 0.01). So each prediction is just "this book's average, minus your usual harshness."
2. **The averages differ by noise.** On Goodreads as a whole, *The Magic Mountain* and *Buddenbrooks* both average **4.14**. But the model uses averages from the dataset's own readers: 274 for *Magic Mountain* (average 3.96) and 150 for *Buddenbrooks* (4.21). That 0.25 gap is small-sample noise, not a real difference.
3. **Calibration multiplies that noise by about 4.** Your raw predictions sit in a narrow band (standard deviation 0.27), while your actual ratings spread across 1–5 (standard deviation 1.05). Calibration stretches the first onto the second so predictions span your real rating range. That's the change you asked for earlier, so that not everything shows as 3.4-ish. Here it turns a noise gap of 0.25 into a 1.25★ gap.

Stretching that much would only be justified if raw predictions tracked your ratings closely. They correlate at only 0.43 with your actual ratings, and a statistically honest stretch would be about **1.7×, not 3.8×**. So the calibration is overconfident, most of all for books like these where it has nothing personal to go on. Your 5★ for *The Magic Mountain* is exactly the kind of case it gets wrong.

**Possible fixes:**
- **Stretch personal evidence, not book averages** (my recommendation): calibrate only the part of the prediction that comes from your own ratings, and use a gentler stretch for the book-average part. Books with real evidence would still spread out, while unconnected books would stay near "average adjusted for you". Here, all three Mann novels would land around 3.3–3.6.
- **Cap the overall stretch using the correlation** (about 1.7× for you): simpler, but it compresses all predictions again. That partly undoes the spread you wanted.
- **Use Goodreads' global averages** (millions of ratings) rather than the dataset's for well-known books. This would remove the noise in point 2. It combines well with either fix above.

Any of these changes the displayed ratings and the prediction floor, so I'd measure the rating accuracy (RMSE) and ranking effects before switching. Want me to try the first option together with Goodreads averages, and show you the before and after?

2. **Stretch only personal evidence (the first option).** Each book gets the calibration stretch in proportion to how strongly it's linked to books you've rated. Books with no links stay unstretched. Displayed predictions miss held-out ratings by **0.87 stars on average**, down from 0.99 before, nearly as accurate as uncalibrated predictions. The old 4.8s were inflated by the same over-stretching as *Magic Mountain*'s 2.64, just in the other direction. # Plan: Visible prompt and commit history, DECISIONS.md, and a changelog page

## Context
Shelf Life was built almost entirely through conversation with Claude Code. The user wants that process visible and permanent:
- every prompt, Claude's replies and the commits logged in the repo;
- a public **changelog page** that shows them linearly or grouped by category;
- a **DECISIONS.md** of the choices made along the way.

All of this starts retroactively and must keep happening automatically. Going forward, commits should be small, with clear, descriptive messages.

**User's decisions:**
- `prompts/` holds each prompt plus Claude's final reply. Tool calls and command output are left out, and pasted files and screenshots become short placeholders.
- `DECISIONS.md` and `prompts/` live in the Shelf Life folder.
- The changelog page is reached from the About page and a footer link, not the top nav.

**Source material:**
- **Transcripts** in `~/.claude/projects/-Users-mattroth-Desktop-GitHub-projects/`:
  - the main session `fe7c091a…`: 92 typed prompts in about 68 MB of JSONL, plus 7 inputs given through tool interactions (answers to questions, plan comments, plan rejections with feedback);
  - two tiny earlier sessions.
- **Git:** 17 Shelf Life commits (merges included), touching `New & Improved Goodreads Book Recommender/` before the rename and `01 - Shelf Life (Goodreads Recommender v2)/` after it.

## Categories (shared by prompts, commits and decisions)
`ui` UI/UX · `model` Recommender model · `eval` Evaluation · `data` Data & pipeline · `assistant` AI Assistant · `infra` Infrastructure & deploy · `docs` Docs & repo · `discussion` Questions/explanations (prompts only)

## 1. Export past conversations → `prompts/` (`scripts/export_prompts.py`)
- **Input and output:** reads one transcript JSONL and writes `prompts/<YYYY-MM-DD>_<session8>.md`. Re-running regenerates the same file.
- **Each entry has:**
  - an id `<session8>-<n>` and a timestamp;
  - the user text, including inputs from tool interactions, labelled "Answer to Claude's question" or "Comment on plan";
  - Claude's **final** reply text for that turn, without interim status text or tool calls.
- **Cleaning:**
  - Skip system reminders, compaction summaries, interrupted turns and empty prompts.
  - Replace pasted documents with `[attached file: name, N lines]` and images with `[screenshot]`.
  - Shorten local path prefixes (`` → repo-relative).
- **Index:** writes `prompts/index.json` (id, session, time, short title) for the page builder.
- **Categories:** `prompts/categories.json` maps prompt id → categories. I'll label the roughly 100 past prompts by hand. Unlabeled ones show as "uncategorized", and the build warns about them.
- **Run now** on all three sessions.

## 2. Keep it automatic: Claude Code hook
- **Where:** a new shared `projects/.claude/settings.json`, committed. The existing `settings.local.json` stays local.
- **Hook:** a `Stop` hook runs `export_prompts.py --from-hook`, which reads `transcript_path` from the hook's stdin JSON. After every turn, the current session's file in `prompts/` is refreshed.
- **Cost:** parsing the 68 MB transcript takes about 1–2 s per turn. The script streams the file and only writes when the content changed.

## 3. `DECISIONS.md` (Shelf Life folder)
- **Format:** one entry per decision:
  - date and category;
  - **Decision**, **Context**, **Alternatives considered**, **Why**;
  - links to the prompt id(s) and commit(s).
- **Retroactive entries (about 30)**, drawn from the prompts and commits. For example:
  - same UCSD data, hybrid item-item + ALS, genres from reader shelves instead of LDA;
  - no per-author cap; no ubiquity correction ("finger on the scales");
  - YA hidden by default (threshold 0.22); prediction floor at average − 0.25; stable ranks under filters;
  - fame-gated prediction boost (δ 0.75, 316k ratings);
  - item means shrunk toward Goodreads averages, because outright replacement was worse;
  - evidence-gated calibration (K = 0.1);
  - Assistant: Sonnet 5 + web search, Haiku/Sonnet routing, owner's key with caps;
  - Cloud Run with scale to zero; repo order; public demo library; homepage two-button flow.
- **Where the reasoning comes from:** the measured numbers come from the eval runs recorded in those conversations. Where a reason isn't on record, I'll say so rather than invent one.

## 4. Changelog data (`scripts/build_changelog.py` → `frontend/src/changelog.json`)
- **Commits:** read from `git log` over both Shelf Life paths and the root README, with hash, date, subject, body, files changed and categories.
  - Past commits use a hand-made `prompts/commit_categories.json` (hash → categories).
  - Future commits get their category from the message prefix.
  - Merge commits are folded into their branch.
- **Prompts:** read from `prompts/index.json` and the session files. Each prompt is linked to the commits made after it and before the next prompt in the same session.
- **Decisions:** `DECISIONS.md` is parsed into entries with categories and links.
- **When it runs:** from `make frontend` and `make deploy`, like `scripts/code_links.py`. The output file is committed like `codeLinks.json`, because Cloud Build has no `.git`.

## 5. Changelog page (`frontend/src/pages/ChangelogPage.tsx`, lazy-loaded like About)
- **Route:** `view=changelog` (`useUrlState.ts`). Links: "How this was built →" on the About page and "Changelog" in the footer (`App.tsx`).
- **Three views** (toggle):
  - **Timeline:** prompts and commits interleaved by time, each prompt followed by its commits;
  - **By category:** grouped sections;
  - **Decisions:** the DECISIONS.md entries.
- **Shared controls:** category filter chips and text search.
- **Prompt cards:** the prompt text, an expandable Claude reply, category chips, and links to its commits.
- **Commit cards:** short hash (link to GitHub), message, body, files changed.
- **Markdown:** move the safe renderer out of `ChatPage.tsx` into `components/Markdown.tsx` so both pages can use it.

## 6. Conventions going forward (CLAUDE.md + memory)
- **Small commits**, one concern each.
- **Message format:** `<category>: <imperative summary>` (≤ 72 chars, categories above), with a body that says what changed and why.
- **Decisions:** add a DECISIONS.md entry whenever a choice or tradeoff is made, linking the prompt id.
- **Prompt files:** commit the auto-exported `prompts/` files with related work, and label new prompt ids in `prompts/categories.json` at commit time.
- **Memory:** save a feedback memory with these rules.

## Shipping (this task's own commits follow the new rules)
- **Branch:** `br-changelog`, with small commits:
  1. `docs: add prompt export script and past conversations`
  2. `docs: add DECISIONS.md with retroactive decisions`
  3. `infra: add Stop hook to export prompts automatically`
  4. `docs: categorize past prompts and commits`
  5. `infra: build changelog data from git and prompts`
  6. `ui: add changelog page with timeline, category and decision views`
  7. `docs: document commit and decision conventions`
- **Push the branch and stop there.** Merging and deploying wait for the user's go-ahead.

## Critical files
- **New:**
  - `scripts/export_prompts.py`, `scripts/build_changelog.py`
  - `prompts/` (session files, `index.json`, `categories.json`, `commit_categories.json`), `DECISIONS.md`
  - `frontend/src/pages/ChangelogPage.tsx`, `frontend/src/components/Markdown.tsx`, `frontend/src/changelog.json`
  - `projects/.claude/settings.json`
- **Modified:**
  - `Makefile` (`frontend` and `deploy` run the build script)
  - `App.tsx` (route, footer link), `useUrlState.ts`, `AboutPage.tsx` (link), `ChatPage.tsx` (import the shared Markdown renderer)
  - `CLAUDE.md`, `styles.css`

## Verification
1. **Export:** spot-check the exported files against the transcript:
   - the count of prompts plus tool-interaction inputs is 92 + 7;
   - pasted CSVs and screenshots are placeholders;
   - no system reminders or tool output leak through;
   - grep for `sk-ant`, the email address and the long local path prefix.
2. **Hook:** run the hook command by hand with a sample stdin JSON. It regenerates the session file, and a second run makes no changes.
3. **Tests:** `tests/test_changelog.py` covers:
   - the exporter on a small synthetic transcript (prompt, tool-interaction answer, interim versus final reply, attachment placeholder);
   - prompt↔commit linking by time;
   - DECISIONS.md parsing;
   - plus the full pytest suite.
4. **Browser:** the changelog page in all three views, filters, search and expand/collapse; the links from About and the footer; mobile layout; no console errors.
5. **Commits:** `git log` on the branch shows the small `category:` commits; push the branch only.

</details>

# Plan: Visual milestone timeline on the Changelog page

## Context
The Changelog page is comprehensive (80 prompts, 35 commits, 36 decisions), but it's hard to take in. The user wants to keep it, and add a **visual, navigable timeline of major project changes** above it:
- Hovering a milestone pops up the prompts and Claude's responses that led to the change, with links to the commits.
- I choose which changes earn a milestone.
- If they don't fit, use horizontal scroll or shrinking icons.

## Milestones (curated, 18)
Stored in a new hand-maintained `prompts/milestones.json`, the same kind of curated metadata as `categories.json`. Each entry has:
- `id`, `date`, `title` (short), `summary` (1–2 sentences), `category`, `icon` (emoji);
- `prompts` (ids), `commits` (short hashes), `decisions` (D-ids).

Only kept (non-omitted) prompt ids are used (F = `fe7c091a-`, W = `ec278335-`). The build script warns if a milestone references a missing prompt, commit or decision.

## Data (`scripts/build_changelog.py`)
- Load `prompts/milestones.json` and add it to `changelog.json` as `milestones`.
- Commits are resolved by short-hash prefix to full URLs; unknown references are warned about and dropped.
- Prompts and decisions are referenced by id; the page looks them up in the existing arrays.

## UI (`frontend/src/components/MilestoneTimeline.tsx`, rendered at the top of `ChangelogPage`, above the view controls)
- **Track:** a horizontal line with 18 evenly spaced nodes, each a category-colored circle with the milestone's emoji, the date and a two-line short title (about 150 px per node).
  - The track is wider than the page, so it **scrolls horizontally**, with snap points, ‹ › arrow buttons and edge fades (the same pattern as the Recommendations tab strip).
  - Day labels mark where each day starts. A "5 days later" break sits between Sep 28 and Oct 3. Spacing is even rather than proportional to time, because most work happened in three days.
- **Popover:** opens on hover or keyboard focus (desktop), and on tap (mobile).
  - It's positioned with `position: fixed` from the node's bounding rectangle, so the scroll container can't clip it. It flips above or below to stay on screen, stays open while the pointer is over it (short close delay), and closes on Escape or an outside click.
  - **Content:** title, date, category chip, summary, then each prompt (kind label, prompt text clamped to a few lines, and an expandable "Claude's reply" using the shared `components/Markdown.tsx`), then commit links (short hash plus subject, to GitHub), plus decision chips.
  - Max height about 60vh, scrolling inside.
- **Navigation:** "Show in changelog" switches the list below to the Timeline view and scrolls to and flashes the milestone's first prompt, reusing the existing `goPrompt` / `focus` logic in `ChangelogPage.tsx`. Decision chips switch to the Decisions view and scroll to that decision.
- **Phones:** the same horizontal scroll with smaller nodes; tapping a node opens the popover as a bottom sheet.
- **Accessibility:** nodes are buttons with `aria-expanded`; the popover is a labelled dialog region.
- **Styles:** in `styles.css`, reusing the category colors (`.cl-<category>` `--c` variables) and chip styles.

## Docs
- **CLAUDE.md** (Working conventions): when a change is significant, add or extend a milestone in `prompts/milestones.json`.
- **DECISIONS.md:** no entry; this is presentation, not a product decision.

## Shipping
Small commits on `br-changelog`, then push (no merge or deploy):
1. `docs: curate project milestones for the changelog timeline`
2. `infra: include milestones in the changelog data`
3. `ui: add a milestone timeline above the changelog`
4. `docs: note milestone upkeep in CLAUDE.md`

## Verification
1. **Data:** `python3 scripts/build_changelog.py` reports 18 milestones with no warnings. A new test in `tests/test_changelog.py` checks that every milestone reference resolves.
2. **Browser (Playwright), desktop and 420 px:**
   - the track scrolls, and the arrows and snapping work;
   - hovering a node opens the popover with prompts, a reply, commit links and decisions;
   - the popover stays open when moved into and closes on leave or Escape;
   - "Show in changelog" scrolls to the right prompt;
   - tap opens it on mobile;
   - no console errors.
3. **Tests:** full pytest and a frontend build pass; local server refreshed so the user can view it.

## fe7c091a-108 · 2026-10-03 14:37 UTC

**Prompt**

> awesome! also I notice the favicon is the correct logo when viewing the local deploy but the production version uses a book emoji

**Claude**

The book emoji is coming from your browser's cache, not from the live site. Production serves the same logo files as your local server, byte for byte. Before the logo was added on Sep 28, the favicon was a 📚 emoji, and browsers hold onto favicons long after a site changes them. Your local server never had the emoji, so it shows the logo.

I made two fixes so every returning visitor gets the logo, not just you:
- **Version tag:** the favicon links now end in `?v=2`. Browsers treat that as a new icon and download it fresh.
- **`/favicon.ico`:** browsers and bookmark tools request this address by default, and it returned the app's HTML page. It now returns the logo.

Both work on your local server and the 47 tests pass. I restarted the local server for the second fix, and it still has your API key, so the Assistant works.

The fix is in commit `2f3e5f8`, plus `cb8d308`, which logs the prompt under the logo milestone. It's pushed on `br-timeline-first-open` with the hover-ring change, not merged or deployed. Production will keep showing the emoji to you until it's deployed. To see the logo before then, open `/favicon.png` on the live site once, or clear the site's data in Chrome.
